This page covers the part of cyRAVEN you have to think about yourself: which
cells it keeps, how you tell it what cell types to look for, and how the raw
numbers get put on a sensible scale. Everything else depends on these.

## Throwing away what is not a cell

A cytometry file is not a clean list of cells. It also contains dust, broken
cell fragments, two cells that went through the laser stuck together, and cells
that were already dead. All of these produce measurements, and none of them
should be counted.

cyRAVEN removes them in the same four steps a person would, in the same order.

**Step 1, size and granularity.** Every cell scatters light in two directions:
forward, which tracks roughly with size, and sideways, which tracks with how
grainy the inside of the cell is. Debris is small and scatters little light, so
it sits in a cloud near the origin, separated from real cells by a gap. cyRAVEN
finds that gap and cuts below it.

**Step 2, single cells.** When two cells stick together they pass the laser as
one event and get recorded as one very large cell. They are spotted by comparing
the height of the light pulse with its total area: a doublet takes longer to pass
through, so its pulse is wider without being taller. Events that fall off that
relationship are discarded. `--singlet-mad-k` controls how strict this is.

**Step 3, live cells.** A viability dye only enters cells whose membrane has
already failed, so dead cells stain brightly and are cut off. If your panel does
not include a viability dye, cyRAVEN skips this and tells you it did.

**Step 4, white blood cells.** CD45 is present on all leukocytes and absent on
red cells and platelets, so it separates the cells you want from everything else
that survived the earlier steps. If CD45 is missing from your panel, every live
cell becomes the denominator instead, and the run warns you, because "percent of
white blood cells" and "percent of everything" are different numbers and should
not be compared.

Everything you define later is counted inside the CD45 positive group, so your
frequencies are percentages of white blood cells.

## Why each sample gets its own cut-off

Antibodies do not stain every sample equally. Reagent lots differ, tubes sit for
different lengths of time before they are run, and the cells themselves vary.
The practical result is that the boundary between "negative" and "positive" for a
given protein sits in a slightly different place in every sample.

A cut-off drawn once and copied across a batch ignores that. In a weakly stained
sample it sits too high and throws away real positive cells; in a bright one it
sits too low and lets negatives in.

So for each protein in each sample, cyRAVEN takes the cells that survived the
four steps above, looks at the distribution of that protein, and finds the dip
between the dim group and the bright group. The cut-off goes in the dip. A sample
whose CD4 signal is shifted lower gets a lower cut-off and keeps its CD4 cells.

### Checking the cut-offs it chose

This is the decision that most affects your results, so cyRAVEN writes down every
one of them in `thresholds_used.csv`. Two columns matter.

`threshold` is where the cut landed.

`source` says how it got there. `valley` means a genuine dip was found between
two groups of cells. `quantile_fallback` means there was no dip, and the software
fell back to taking a fixed percentage of the distribution.

A `quantile_fallback` is not automatically wrong, but it means the protein did
not visibly separate positive from negative cells in that sample, so any
frequency that depends on it deserves suspicion. If one protein falls back in
most of your samples, that protein is not working in your panel and no gating
strategy will rescue it.

`threshold_scale_qc.csv` goes further and flags any cut-off that sits far from
where the same protein landed in your other samples. Those are the first ones to
look at.

## Writing a population specification

This is the one input you have to write yourself, and almost everything cyRAVEN
produces depends on it. It goes in the `populations:` block of the file you pass
to `--config`.

```yaml
populations:
  CD4 T cells:
    CD3: above
    CD4: above
    CD8: below
  Central memory CD4:
    CD3: above
    CD4: above
    CD8: below
    CCR7: above
    CD45RA: below
```

Read the first entry as a sentence: a CD4 T cell is a cell that has CD3, has CD4,
and does not have CD8. That is the same definition an immunologist would give,
written in a form the software can apply. A cell joins the population only if it
satisfies every line, checked against that sample's own cut-offs.

Three directions are available.

`above` and `below` mean the protein is present or absent.

`intermediate` is for proteins that come at three levels rather than two. CD14 on
monocytes is the standard example: classical monocytes are CD14 bright,
intermediate monocytes sit in the middle, and non-classical monocytes are
CD14 dim. For these, cyRAVEN looks for a second dip inside the positive cells to
find the upper edge of the middle group. If there is no second dip, it reports
the population as unavailable rather than silently lumping the middle cells in
with the bright ones.

### Four steps to writing one

1. Find out what your panel actually contains. Any run writes
   `thresholds_used.csv`, which lists every marker it resolved. The `$PnS` field
   of any file in the batch has the same information.
2. Write the top-level lineages first and check they score sensibly before adding
   subsets. If CD3 is wrong, every T cell subset below it is wrong too.
3. Pass the file with `--config my_panel.yaml`. The same file can also hold
   colour choices, threshold overrides and metadata translations, all optional.
4. Read the run log. Any population whose markers are not all in the panel is
   reported as UNAVAILABLE and scored as nothing. An empty frequency table is
   almost always a spelling difference between your specification and the `$PnS`
   field, not a missing population.

Copy `system.file("config", "config_cohorts.yaml", package = "cyRAVEN")` for the
overall shape of the file and replace the populations with your own.

### If you skip the config

The built-in specification describes a myeloid and lymphoid panel: CD14, CD16,
CD19, CD56 with NKG2D, CD127 with CD25, and the gamma delta T cell receptors. On
any other panel most of it reports UNAVAILABLE. A T cell panel of CD3, CD4, CD8,
CD38, HLA-DR, CCR7 and CD45RA overlaps it in three populations out of fifteen.
Treat the built-in one as a worked example, not a default that will fit you.

### Why the specification is not learned from the data

You could imagine cyRAVEN looking at your samples and proposing the populations
itself. It deliberately does not. A specification fitted to the same samples it
is then tested against cannot be contradicted by them, and contradiction is the
whole point of the threshold drift check, the phenotype heatmap and the gate
against cluster comparison.

What the data is allowed to do is propose. `--explain-clusters` takes any cluster
your specification does not describe and learns a short sequence of two-marker
gates that selects those cells, with performance measured on cells held out of
the fit. The result goes to `cluster_gate_proposals.csv`. Deciding which of those
becomes a named population is your job, and next run's specification is a file
you edited by hand.

## Putting the numbers on a readable scale

Raw fluorescence values span an enormous range. A negative cell might read 30 and
a bright one 200,000, so plotted directly the negatives collapse into a line
against the axis and you cannot see where one group ends and the next begins.
Every cytometry tool therefore rescales the data first, and the choice of scale
affects where the cut-offs end up.

cyRAVEN offers two.

**arcsinh** (the default) compresses the bright end while leaving the dim end
spread out. It needs one number, the cofactor, which sets how much of the
near-zero region gets stretched. The usual published value of 5 comes from mass
cytometry and is wrong for most fluorescence data, so cyRAVEN measures a suitable
value from your own files instead of assuming one.

**logicle** (`--transform logicle`) is the flow cytometry convention. It behaves
linearly near zero, which matters because correcting for optical bleed between
channels pushes some genuinely negative cells below zero. arcsinh has nowhere to
put those; logicle does.

One detail is worth knowing. cyRAVEN works out the logicle settings once for the
whole panel and applies them to every sample. Some tools fit them separately for
each file, which puts every sample on a slightly different scale and makes
comparing brightness between samples meaningless.

### The choice changes your answer

This is not a cosmetic setting. On a seven-colour T cell panel, the major
populations came out within 0.1% of each other under both transforms, but the
CCR7 and CD45RA memory subsets moved by tens of percent.

The reason is visible in `thresholds_used.csv`. CCR7 is a dim marker with no
clean separation. Under arcsinh, the software found a real dip in some samples
and had to fall back to a quantile in others, so the cut-off jumped around. Under
logicle it found a dip every time.

The lesson generalises: for dim proteins with no obvious negative and positive
groups, the scale decides whether a stable cut-off exists at all. Check the
`source` column before trusting a memory subset frequency.

`--transform none` leaves the values alone, for data that has already been
transformed elsewhere.

## Correcting for colour bleed

Fluorescent dyes emit across a range of wavelengths, so light from one dye leaks
into the detector meant for another. Left uncorrected, a cell bright for one
protein looks mildly positive for several others it does not actually have.

The correction is calculated on the instrument from single-stain controls and
saved inside the FCS file. cyRAVEN applies it when it is there and tells you when
it is not.

It will not calculate one for you. That belongs in the acquisition software,
where you can see the controls and check the result, and applying a correction
twice is as damaging as never applying it.
